reply.summary: E0 (initial_measurements.json) shows similar t=0 segmented empty-area fractions in A and B, followed by lower values in A (~0.0044 at 24 h) and increasing B values (~0.0892 at 24 h). These are image area fractions, not concentrations or free energies; seven fields are nested within two preparations. Candidate C1 proposes that B develops internal RNA-poor cavities when transcription-driven junction accumulation outruns network relaxation, trapping solvent-rich regions that then become mechanically arrested. This is an explicitly new, unconfirmed mechanism hypothesis, not an inference from the area-fraction curve. Reduced state x is load-bearing junction density (dimensionless effective fraction); r(t) is transcriptional production flux per droplet volume (h^-1 in this reduced model); tau is network relaxation time (h). Adopt xdot = alpha r(t) - x/tau, with alpha dimensionless. Define arrest threshold x_c and cavity state q: qdot = k_n max(x-x_c,0) - k_d q while x < x_c, and qdot = 0 after x first reaches x_c (arrest). Here q is cavity area fraction, k_n and k_d have units h^-1, and the post-threshold freeze is a proposed reduced rule, not established physics. It predicts a rate/history effect: at equal integrated production, a sufficiently fast pulse can cross x_c while a slow schedule does not; after arrest, q persists when production falls. Meaningful alternative C_alt is equilibrium composition-driven demixing: after matching final composition and allowing equilibration, cavity fraction should not depend on production schedule. E0 alone cannot distinguish these, identify x, show arrest, or establish amplification as causal.

reply.summary: R1_S1 (abstract only, 2024-12-15) reports metadynamics simulations in which slow sticker exchange kinetically arrests sticker-spacer condensate coalescence, while faster exchange at similar saturation permits merger; it does not address RNA loop junctions, cavity formation, or transcription coupling. R1_S3 (abstract only, 2023-06-29) reports gel-like kinetic trapping from percolated beta-sheet networks in proteins with at least two LARKS; this is chemically distinct. R1_S2 is a review on condensate effects on reaction pathways, and R1_S4 concerns electrostatics and charge-rich condensate phase modeling; neither provides the missing mechanism. E1 existing preparation-1 summary: B n=279 tracks, median final squared displacement 1.596 um2, median 98 frames, selected top-100 median 123.048 um2; A n=838, median 0.636 um2, median 159 frames, selected top-100 median 19.583 um2. The unequal durations and selected-tail statistic do not support uniform immobilization; they are compatible with heterogeneity or selection and do not establish cavity-specific arrest. H1 remains an explicit unconfirmed bridge hypothesis. Search R2 is issued for RNA self-complementary/kissing-loop exchange and network connectivity.

candidates.target: Delayed emergence and persistence of internal RNA-poor cavity area in transcribing RNA droplets, especially the B/A contrast.
known_relations: E0: mean segmented area fraction A=.01487 and B=.01381 at t=0; at 24 h A=.00446 and B=.08918. Pooled fields are not independent preparation-level inference.
R1_S1 abstract: slow sticker exchange can arrest simulated sticker-spacer condensate coalescence; faster exchange at similar saturation allows merger. No target RNA or cavity mechanism.
R1_S3 abstract: multiple LARKS can form percolated beta-sheet networks and kinetically trap protein condensates; chemistry differs from RNA loop junctions.
R1_S2 review abstract mentions both enhancement and inhibition of reactions in condensates, including diffusion retardation; not cavity mechanism evidence.
R1_S4 abstract concerns electrostatic effects and coarse-grained phase predictions for charge-rich condensates; ionic/composition variables remain possible alternatives.

E1 existing prep-1 summary: B n=279, median final squared displacement 1.596 um2, median 98 frames, selected top-100 median 123.048 um2; A n=838, median .636 um2, median 159 frames, selected top-100 median 19.583 um2. Unequal track durations and selected tail limit interpretation.
hypotheses: H1 (new, unconfirmed): production of associative RNA creates a percolating population of loop-mediated junctions whose exchange is slow relative to production and stress relaxation; threshold crossing traps internal solvent-rich domains. This is a new bridge hypothesis, not established in target material.
H1a (unverified bridge): terminal self-complementary RNA loops act as exchangeable stickers, and slow exchange plus sufficient connectivity can produce long-lived viscoelastic arrest.
H2 alternative: amplification-linked composition/product heterogeneity changes equilibrium phase coexistence; at matched composition after equilibration schedule history does not matter.
H3 alternative: reaction carryover or imaging/segmentation differences cause some or all of the contrast.

gaps.description: Whether reversible RNA loop junctions have exchange and connectivity conditions capable of arresting this network, and whether production rate can cross a threshold that traps internal cavities. R1 supports generic arrest analogies only in other condensate systems.
Amplification effects on template/product heterogeneity versus reaction carryover remain unresolved.
Tracking summaries do not resolve cavity-specific mobility, coarsening, or arrest; network state, relaxation, and phase composition are unmeasured.

candidates.observation_mapping: E0 is segmented dark internal area divided by filled-droplet area. E1 summarizes displacement and track duration, not direct relaxation or cavity-specific coarsening. Neither identifies x, tau, composition, or RNA concentration.
alternatives: H2 equilibrium composition-driven demixing; schedule-independent after matched composition and equilibration.
H3 amplification-related carryover changes transcription or imaging.
H4 segmentation, denominator, track-duration censoring, or selected-tail effects produce apparent mobility/area differences.
predictions: At equal integrated production and matched final composition, H1 predicts different q only when the faster schedule crosses x_c; H2 predicts convergence after equilibration.
If threshold arrest occurs, cavity-specific coarsening should plateau after crossing; E1 cannot establish this because track durations differ and selected tail is not a population trajectory.

Conditional 36-48 h commitment inherited from L2: if arrest occurred in B by 24 h, mean B area fraction stays above A at 36 and 48 h and grows more slowly than over 12-24 h; conditional and not revised by E1.
checks: Units: alpha*r and x/tau are h^-1; qdot terms are h^-1.
At r=0, x decays exponentially with tau; if below x_c there is no threshold-generated q.
R1_S1 is an abstract-level simulation of coalescence, not RNA cavity nucleation; R1_S3 is protein-specific beta-sheet aging. Transfer to RNA loops and transcription remains an added hypothesis.
Post-threshold freeze stipulates persistence and requires direct cavity-specific motion/coarsening evidence.

E1 B has shorter median tracks (98 vs 159 frames) and much larger selected top-100 displacement than A (123.048 vs 19.583 um2), despite smaller median displacement; this contradicts a simple all-B-immobile account and may reflect heterogeneity/selection.
E1 provides no uncertainty, track-level distribution, cavity identity validation, or duration-matched comparison; no inferential statistic is calculated.
evidence_conflicts: E0 is compatible with delayed B cavity emergence but does not identify mechanism or causal effect.
E1 selected-tail mobility is higher in B while median mobility is modestly higher and median track duration shorter; uniform arrest is not supported.
Generic R1 analogies support possible exchange-limited/percolation arrest elsewhere, not RNA loop exchange, cavity formation, or production coupling.

sources.title: Separation of sticker-spacer energetics governs the coalescence of metastable condensates.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: Biological condensates often emerge as a multidroplet state and never coalesce into one large droplet within the experimental timespan. Previous work revealed that the sticker-spacer architecture of biopolymers may dynamically stabilize the multidroplet state. Here, we simulate the condensate coalescence using metadynamics approach and reveal two distinct physical mechanisms underlying the fusion of droplets. Condensates made of sticker-spacer polymers readily undergo a kinetic arrest when stickers exhibit slow exchange while fast exchanging stickers at similar levels of saturation allow merger to equilibrium states. On the other hand, condensates composed of homopolymers fuse readily until they reach a threshold density. Increase in entropy upon intercondensate mixing of chains drives the fusion of sticker-spacer chains. We map the range of mechanisms of kinetic arrest from slow sticker exchange dynamics to density mediated in terms of energetic separation of stickers and spacers. Our predictions appear to be in qualitative agreement with recent experiments probing dynamic nature of protein-RNA condensates.

sources.title: Toward Design Principles for Biomolecular Condensates for Metabolic Pathways.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: Biology uses membrane-less organelles or biomolecular condensates as dynamic reaction compartments that can form or dissolve to regulate biochemical pathways. This has led to a flurry of research aiming to design new synthetic organelles that function as reaction crucibles for enzymes and biomolecular cascades in biotechnology. The mechanisms by which a condensate can enhance multistep biochemical processes including mass action, tuning the chemical environment, scaffolding and metabolic channelling is reviewed. These mechanisms are not inherently beneficial for the rate of enzymatic processes but can also inhibit a reaction. Similarly, some aspects of condensates are likely intrinsically inhibitory including retardation of diffusion, where the net effect of a condensate will be a trade-off between inhibitory and stimulatory effects. It is discussed which generalizable conclusions can be drawn so far and how close it is to design principles for condensates for enzyme cascades in microbial cell factories including which reactions are likely to be enhanced by condensates and which type of condensate will be suited for which reaction.

sources.title: Location and Concentration of Aromatic-Rich Segments Dictates the Percolating Inter-Molecular Network and Viscoelastic Properties of Ageing Condensates.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: Maturation of functional liquid-like biomolecular condensates into solid-like aggregates has been linked to the onset of several neurodegenerative disorders. Low-complexity aromatic-rich kinked segments (LARKS) contained in numerous RNA-binding proteins can promote aggregation by forming inter-protein β-sheet fibrils that accumulate over time and ultimately drive the liquid-to-solid transition of the condensates. Here, atomistic molecular dynamics simulations are combined with sequence-dependent coarse-grained models of various resolutions to investigate the role of LARKS abundance and position within the amino acid sequence in the maturation of condensates. Remarkably, proteins with tail-located LARKS display much higher viscosity over time than those in which the LARKS are placed toward the center. Yet, at very long timescales, proteins with a single LARKS-independently of its location-can still relax and form high viscous liquid condensates. However, phase-separated condensates of proteins containing two or more LARKS become kinetically trapped due to the formation of percolated β-sheet networks that display gel-like behavior. Furthermore, as a work case example, they demonstrate how shifting the location of the LARKS-containing low-complexity domain of FUS protein toward its center effectively precludes the accumulation of β-sheet fibrils in FUS-RNA condensates, maintaining functional liquid-like behavior without ageing.

sources.title: Chemically Informed Coarse-Graining of Electrostatic Forces in Charge-Rich Biomolecular Condensates.
sources.scope: abstract only; historical publication metadata verified, historical abstract text version not independently archived
sources.original_evidence: Biomolecular condensates composed of highly charged biomolecules, such as DNA, RNA, chromatin, and nucleic-acid binding proteins, are ubiquitous in the cell nucleus. The biophysical properties of these charge-rich condensates are largely regulated by electrostatic interactions. Residue-resolution coarse-grained models that describe solvent and ions implicitly are widely used to gain mechanistic insights into the biophysical properties of condensates, offering transferability, computational efficiency, and accurate predictions for multiple systems. However, their predictive accuracy diminishes for charge-rich condensates due to the implicit treatment of solvent and ions. Here, we present Mpipi-Recharged, a residue-resolution coarse-grained model that improves the description of charge effects in biomolecular condensates containing disordered proteins, multidomain proteins, and/or disordered single-stranded RNAs. Mpipi-Recharged introduces a pair-specific asymmetric Yukawa electrostatic potential, informed by atomistic simulations. We show that this asymmetric coarse-graining of electrostatic forces captures intricate effects, such as charge blockiness, stoichiometry variations in complex coacervates, and modulation of salt concentration, without requiring explicit solvation. Mpipi-Recharged provides excellent agreement with experiments in predicting the phase behavior of highly charged condensates. Overall, Mpipi-Recharged improves the computational tools available to investigate the physicochemical mechanisms regulating biomolecular condensates, enhancing the scope of computer simulations in this field.
